claims.claim: Starship Flight 15 is targeted no earlier than Friday, November 13, 2026, with a 75-minute window opening at 4:45 p.m. CT / 5:45 p.m. ET and closing at 6:00 p.m. CT.
claims.episode_span: targeted no earlier than Friday, November 13, with a seventy-five-minute window opening at 4:45 p.m. Central Time, 5:45 p.m. Eastern, and closing at 6:00 p.m. Central
claims.supporting_quote: Targeted no earlier than Friday, Nov 13, 2026, with a 75-minute window opening at 4:45 p.m. CT / 5:45 p.m. ET (closes 6:00 p.m. CT).

claims.claim: SpaceX's Flight 15 mission page stated that launch was pending regulatory approval as of November 7–11, 2026 checks.
claims.episode_span: The launch is pending regulatory approval. That is the wording on the SpaceX mission page as of checks between November 7 and 11.
claims.supporting_quote: FAA licence for Flight 15 Pending regulatory approval

claims.claim: Flight 15 is assigned Booster 22 and Ship 42, both V3 vehicles, with Booster 22 the first V3 Super Heavy planned for a tower catch.
claims.episode_span: The vehicles are Booster 22 and Ship 42, both Block 3, also called V3, hardware. Booster 22 is the first V3 Super Heavy planned for a tower catch.
claims.supporting_quote: is the first Super Heavy V3 booster planned to return to the launch site for catch

claims.claim: Booster 22 completed a full-duration 33-engine static fire on October 25, and Ship 42 completed a six-engine static fire and single-engine deorbit simulation on October 28.
claims.episode_span: Booster 22 completed a full-duration thirty-three-engine static fire on October 25. Ship 42 completed a six-engine static fire and a single-engine deorbit simulation on October 28.
claims.supporting_quote: Both completed static fire testing (B22: 33-engine full-duration Oct 25; S42: 6-engine + single-engine deorbit sim Oct 28).

claims.claim: As of about November 10, 2026, Booster 22 was on the pad for final catch testing, including a squeeze test.
claims.episode_span: As of about November 10, Booster 22 was on the pad for final catch testing, including a squeeze test.
claims.supporting_quote: The booster moved to the launch pad that day and was used for final catch testing, including a suspended squeeze test

claims.claim: The Ship is planned to target about 275 km LEO, fly about 14 orbits over a flight lasting more than 22 hours, with reentry around T+22:10:46 and landing burn/flip/catch around T+22:32:34 if cleared.
claims.episode_span: the Ship targets about 275 kilometers, deploys the twenty-six Starlink V3 satellites, and stays up for about fourteen orbits. That is more than twenty-two hours of flight.
claims.supporting_quote: the ship catch at about T+22:32:34 , after roughly 14 orbits at 275 km

claims.claim: SpaceX plans to attempt the Ship catch only if ship reentry and landing systems are confirmed healthy after on-orbit checks, with ocean contingencies if the catch is called off.
claims.episode_span: the Ship catch will be attempted only if ship systems for reentry and landing are confirmed healthy after those on-orbit checks.
claims.supporting_quote: Attempt only if ship systems (reentry/landing) confirmed healthy post-orbit checks (passively safe suborbital trajectory initially; orbit insertion only if cleared).

claims.claim: Contingency ocean landings are the Gulf of Mexico for the booster and Indian or Pacific Ocean options for the ship.
claims.episode_span: the Super Heavy booster has a Gulf of Mexico ocean landing as contingency; the Ship has Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean options
claims.supporting_quote: Contingency ocean landings (Gulf of Mexico for booster; Indian/Pacific Ocean options for ship) if tower catch called off for any reason.

claims.claim: Elon Musk previously estimated first ship-catch success probability at at least 50 or 60 percent, or more likely than not, if Flight 14 succeeded.
claims.episode_span: he previously estimated first Ship-catch success at “at least 50 or 60 percent,” and on the third-quarter earnings call he said a successful Ship catch was “more likely than not,” if Flight 14 had succeeded.
claims.supporting_quote: estimated the probability of success on the first attempt at "at least 50 or 60 percent"

claims.claim: SpaceX frames Flight 15 as a potential first full recovery of an orbital launch system.
claims.episode_span: SpaceX has framed the flight as a potential first full recovery of an orbital launch system.
claims.supporting_quote: SpaceX frames Flight 15 as potential “first full recovery of an orbital launch system.”

claims.claim: The official webcast is planned to start about 30 minutes before liftoff and continue through the ship catch, via the SpaceX Flight 15 mission page and X @SpaceX.
claims.episode_span: The webcast is planned to start about thirty minutes before liftoff and to continue through the Ship catch.
claims.supporting_quote: Webcast starts ~30 minutes before liftoff; planned to continue through ship catch.

claims.claim: Booster catch on Flight 15 would build on three prior V1 Super Heavy catch successes, while the Ship catch is a first attempt.
claims.episode_span: It builds on three prior V1 booster catches, but it is still a first for this block of hardware.
claims.supporting_quote: Booster catch builds on 3 prior V1 successes. Ship catch is first attempt (higher energy reentry).

claims.claim: A November 10 secondary article claiming the FAA license was already in hand is unconfirmed and conflicts with SpaceX’s pending language.
claims.episode_span: A November 10 secondary article claimed the license was already in hand; that claim is unconfirmed and conflicts with SpaceX’s own “pending” language
claims.supporting_quote: One Nov 10 secondary article claims license “in hand,” but this is unconfirmed by SpaceX’s own “pending” language and treated as [UNCONFIRMED].
